title: Entropy Estimates from Stochastic Interpolants
abstract: We present a general method for estimating entropy differences between arbitrary probability distributions using stochastic interpolants. The marginal distributions which bridge the base and target obey a continuity equation, which allows a straightforward calculation of the entropy difference in terms of an inner product of the probability flow velocity and score fields. This formulation has several advantages: (i) no computationally expensive divergence calculations of either field are required, (ii) the score field need not even be learned directly if model transferability is not required, and (iii) on-the-fly estimates are produced nearly for free during training. When tractable base distributions are chosen (e.g. Gaussian chain, ideal gas, etc.), statistical thermodynamic entropies are then immediately recovered. Notably, the analysis relies only on the definition of the Gibbs-Shannon entropy, rather than any particular statistical mechanical ensemble, so that generalized non-equilibrium entropies may be computed. The method is demonstrated on several systems of increasing complexity: (i) a 40-dimensional Gaussian mixture model, (ii) the classical XY model of N spins arranged in one dimension, (iii) the 13-atom Lennard-Jones cluster, and (iv) an active Brownian polymer.
summary: This paper presents a general and computationally efficient method to estimate the entropy difference between any two probability distributions using stochastic interpolants. By reformulating the calculation in terms of the inner product of the probability flow velocity and the score field, it bypasses difficult divergence calculations. This technique is highly valuable for calculating non-equilibrium entropies in complex physical systems, ranging from classical spin models to active matter.
main_problem: The paper addresses the general problem of estimating entropy differences between two arbitrary probability distributions ($ho_0$ and $ho_1$) characterizing physical systems.
main_result: It derives an efficient formula for the entropy difference ($\Delta S$) based on the inner product of the probability flow velocity ($\mathbf{b}$) and the score field ($\mathbf{s}$), avoiding computationally expensive divergence calculations.
method: The method utilizes stochastic interpolants governed by a continuity equation to define a continuous path between the base and target distributions, allowing the entropy difference to be calculated as a time integral of the expected inner product $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{s}$.
model_or_system: The method is general, relying only on the Gibbs-Shannon entropy definition, and has been demonstrated on complex systems including Gaussian mixture models, the classical XY model, Lennard-Jones clusters, and active Brownian polymers.
key_observables: Entropy difference ($\Delta S$), Free Energy difference ($\Delta F$), Probability Flow Velocity ($\mathbf{b}$), and Score Field ($\mathbf{s}$).
important_parameters: The time parameter $t \in [0, 1]$ defining the interpolation path, and system-specific parameters for the tested models (e.g., polymer constants, interaction strengths).
main_assumptions: The derivation assumes that the probability distribution $ho_t(x)$ varies smoothly with the interpolation parameter $t$.
figures_summary: The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but mention results for several systems (GMM, XY Chain, LJ, Active Polymer) showing good agreement with reference values.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the general framework using stochastic interpolants and the continuity equation to derive the $\Delta S$ formula. It then discusses the computational advantages of the inner product formulation and applies this method to several increasingly complex physical models, including polymer dynamics and lattice models.
why_interesting: While the core focus is on classical statistical mechanics, the reliance on stochastic differential equations and flow modeling connects deeply with modern techniques used in quantum dynamics and open quantum systems, particularly those involving non-equilibrium processes.
